title: 2.1 Parts of Program Memory and Scope

questions.q: What does a variable's scope define in C?
choices: The set of code blocks in which the variable's name is bound to a memory location and can be used
The number of bytes the variable occupies in memory
The data type of the variable
The maximum value the variable can hold
questions.explain: Scope defines when a variable's name has meaning: the code blocks in which the name is bound to (associated with) a memory location and can be used by program code.

questions.q: Given `int change(int amt) { int val; val = g_x; g_x += amt; return val; }`, where can the parameter `amt` be used?
choices: Only by statements inside the body of `change`
Anywhere in the program after `change` is declared
Inside `change` and inside any function that calls `change`
Anywhere, because parameters are stored in the data section
questions.explain: Parameters, like local variables, are in scope only inside the function that defines them.
`max`'s own parameters and local variable are in scope, and global `g_x` is in scope everywhere. `main`'s locals `x` and `result` are in scope only inside `main`.

questions.q: Two different functions, `max` and `change`, can each declare a local variable named `val` without conflict.
questions.explain: Local variables are in scope only inside their own function, so a reference to `val` inside `max` means `max`'s `val`. The `val` belonging to `change` is not in scope there.

questions.q: How do you create a global variable in C?
choices: Declare it outside of any function body
Declare it at the top of `main`
Declare it as a parameter of `main`
questions.explain: Declaring a variable outside of any function body creates a global variable.

questions.q: Two global variables in the same program may share a name as long as they have different types.
questions.explain: Every global variable must have a unique name. Its name identifies one specific storage location for the entire run of the program.

questions.q: A global variable is bound to the same memory location for the entire duration of the program.
questions.explain: Globals stay in scope permanently because they are always bound to one specific memory location.
`total` is a global, so every call to `add` updates the same storage: 1 + 6 + 8 = 15. The local `val` gets fresh storage on each call.
`change` can modify the global `g_x` directly: it saves the old value (10) in `val`, adds 10 to `g_x`, and returns 10. `g_x` is now 20.

questions.q: Which are reasons to use local variables and parameters instead of global variables whenever possible?
choices: The code is easier to debug
It can be more space-efficient, because locals and parameters take up memory only while their function is active
questions.explain: Local variables and parameters make code more modular, general-purpose, and easier to debug, and they take up memory only while their function is active. Any function can read and modify globals.

questions.q: When is stack space for a function's parameters and local variables allocated and deallocated?
choices: Allocated when the function is called; deallocated when the function returns
Allocated when the program starts; deallocated when the program exits
Allocated when the variable is first assigned; deallocated when the program exits
Allocated at compile time; never deallocated
questions.explain: Space for a parameter or local variable is allocated on the stack when the function is called and deallocated when it returns.

questions.q: Each active call of a function gets its own region on the stack that holds space for its parameters and local variables. What is this region called?
questions.explain: Each activation of a function gets a separate stack frame that holds its parameters and local variables.

questions.q: In a recursive function, all of the active recursive calls share one copy of the function's local variables.
questions.explain: Each activation gets its own bindings. Every recursive call has a separate stack frame with its own space for parameters and local variables.

questions.q: A recursive function `int fact(int n)` has been called and is currently 4 calls deep, so 4 activations of `fact` are active and none has returned yet. How many separate copies of the parameter `n` exist on the stack?
questions.explain: Each activation has its own stack frame, so each of the 4 active calls has its own copy of `n`.

questions.q: Which part of a program's memory holds local variables and function parameters?
questions.explain: Local variables and parameters live on the stack, inside the stack frame of the function's activation.

questions.q: Which part of a program's memory holds global variables?
questions.explain: Global variables are stored in the data section, and their storage lasts for the entire run of the program.

questions.q: Which part of a program's memory is used for dynamic memory allocation?
questions.explain: The heap is the part of the address space used for dynamic memory allocation.

questions.q: Where are the instructions for functions such as `main`, `max`, and `change` stored?
questions.explain: A program's instructions are stored in the code section.

questions.q: Like the stack, the data region grows and shrinks as functions are called and return.
questions.explain: The data region does not grow or shrink. Storage for globals lasts for the entire run of the program.

questions.q: Which of these memory regions change in size while the program runs?
questions.explain: The stack grows and shrinks as functions are called and return, and the heap grows as more space is allocated dynamically. The data region stays a fixed size.

questions.q: What is a program's address space?
choices: The storage locations for everything the program needs to run, namely its instructions and data
Only the memory that holds the program's global variables
The set of files the program can open on disk
The region of memory reserved for the operating system
questions.explain: The OS creates the address space when it launches the program. It holds storage for the program's instructions and data and can be thought of as an array of addressable bytes.

questions.q: Which part of a program's address space cannot be used by the running program?
choices: The top of memory, which is reserved for the operating system
questions.explain: The top of a program's memory is reserved for the operating system. The remaining parts can be used by the running program.

questions.q: Why is the stack usually placed near the bottom of memory, at the highest addresses?
choices: Stack space grows and shrinks as functions are called and return, so it needs room to change
The stack holds global variables, which must sit far from the code
Higher addresses are faster to access
The operating system region is always at the highest addresses
questions.explain: The stack grows and shrinks during execution, so placing it at the highest addresses leaves room for it to change.

questions.q: As a running program allocates more dynamic memory, which direction does the heap grow?
choices: It does not grow; its size is fixed at launch
questions.explain: The heap is usually far from the stack and grows toward higher addresses as more space is allocated dynamically.
